newsitem.title: INDIA: India government asks states' help in truck strike.
newsitem.headline: India government asks states' help in truck strike.

text.p: The India government has asked states to prepare to intervene after two million striking truck owners kept their vehicles off the roads for a third day, a senior government official said on Thursday.
The movement of goods on roads and through ports and air cargo terminals has been hit, transport officials said.
"We have asked states to intervene and make arrangements for movement of goods and services," Yogendra Narain, the highest ranking civil servant in the Surface Transport Ministry, told Reuters.
"They have been asked to deploy buses, light commercial vehicles and provide protection to those who want to operate their trucks."
The government's stance evoked a caustic response from truck owners who launched the strike on Tuesday in protest against a service tax and surge in insurance premiums.
The protest has kept some 2.2 million trucks off the roads and crippled ground transport of goods.
"These actions of the officials may provoke a sharp reaction from the transporters," S.P. Singh, a spokesman for All India Motor Transport Congress (AIMTC), told Reuters.
"The strike will continue till our demands are met."

The AIMTC represents owners of about two million heavy trucks, one million light and medium-weight trucks and some 60,000 booking and delivery companies. Truckers move about 60 percent of India's goods.
The AIMTC objects to a five percent service tax on road transport which Finance Minister P. Chidambaram proposed in the federal budget for the 1997/98 (April-March) financial year.
It also opposes a decision by state-owned insurance companies which the transport congress said would raise insurance premiums between 300 and 400 percent.
The government has offered to refer the issue of service tax to a panel of parliament deputies and also keep the rise in insurance premiums in abeyance.

"We don't want promises. We want the government to drop the service tax and also drop the hike in insurance premiums," Singh said, predicting that owners of bus and light commercial vehicles would soon join the strike.
Industry and trade associations have urged the truck owners to call off the strike which has severely affected movement of goods and is pushing up prices of essential and perishable commodities.
"The ports have been affected. In Bombay, it has been fully affected," said Narain. On the eastern coast, the ports have been partially affected, he added.
The transport industry was suffering a loss of four billion rupees ($112 million) each day, AIMTC's Singh said.

"The industry would be further crippled and in several cases production would come to a grinding halt if the strike continued even for a few days more," the Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry of India said in a statement.
The supply of aviation fuel could be also affected if the strike lingered for a few more days, industry sources said.
"It is difficult to assess the overall impact on the economy. But it is definitely affecting the economy," said Narain. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
